vmo2-bt-broadband-row.headline: Virgin Media O2 accuses BT of 'choking off' broadband competition
vmo2-bt-broadband-row.body_md:
Britain's second-largest broadband company has picked a public fight with the operator of the network most of the country still depends on. Virgin Media O2 has told the regulator Ofcom that BT's infrastructure arm, Openreach, is trying to "choke off" broadband competition — not through outright refusal, but through a wave of discounts aimed at keeping rival internet service providers loyal to Openreach's pipes.

The discounts in question are aimed at companies such as Vodafone, Sky and TalkTalk, which buy wholesale access to broadband networks and resell it to households under their own brands. Openreach wants those providers to keep routing new full-fibre customers through its network rather than switching to Virgin Media O2's, which is trying to establish itself as a genuine wholesale alternative for the first time. In a submission to Ofcom, which must approve the pricing plan before it can take effect, Virgin Media O2 argues the offer is a calculated move to lock in customers before a rival network can get off the ground.

## A rebate war over rival loyalty

The scheme is an extension of Openreach's existing "Equinox" wholesale pricing programme, which already discounts full-fibre rental for providers who commit most of their new orders to Openreach rather than legacy copper lines or competing fibre builders. The newest addition, due to run from October 2026 for six months, offers a £50 connection rebate to internet providers that sign up incremental new-to-Openreach fibre customers specifically inside Virgin Media O2's own coverage areas — but only to providers already placing at least 1,000 fibre orders a month nationwide, a threshold that effectively limits the offer to the largest resellers.

![Openreach engineer working on a telegraph pole](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e2/BT_Openreach_Engineer_Up_Pole_2012_May_09.JPG)

Virgin Media O2's chief executive, Lutz Schüler, put the complaint in blunter terms than a regulatory filing usually allows. "For BT, it seems Ofcom's conclusions were heard as a dinner bell to start feasting on fibre challengers," he said, calling the discounts "a prime example of a dominant force flexing its muscles to squeeze out emerging competition." Openreach's chief executive, Katie Milligan, rejected the framing entirely: "Ofcom has said that Openreach should be allowed to compete, and we agree," she said, describing the targeted rebates as an effort to "test the waters" in areas where a rival network already exists — precisely the areas Virgin Media O2 needs to win business to make its wholesale ambitions pay off.

## Building a challenger while fending one off

The timing explains the sharpness of the complaint. Virgin Media O2 is midway through a £2 billion acquisition of altnet operator Netomnia, engineered through nexfibre — its joint venture with parent companies Liberty Global and Telefónica — that would knit together roughly 8 million premises of full-fibre coverage by the end of 2027. The pitch to regulators and investors has been consistent: this is meant to be the first wholesale network with the scale to genuinely challenge Openreach's dominance, rather than another niche builder Openreach can wait out.

That deal is itself under regulatory strain. The Competition and Markets Authority referred the Netomnia acquisition for an in-depth Phase 2 investigation in early July, fast-tracked at the parties' own request, citing roughly 80% overlap between the two companies' networks. A verdict is due by 15 December under the CMA's statutory deadline. Virgin Media O2 is therefore arguing on two regulatory fronts at once — trying to persuade the CMA that combining with Netomnia will sharpen competition rather than dull it, while telling Ofcom that Openreach is exploiting the exact period of vulnerability created by that unresolved merger review.

![Openreach fibre broadband street cabinet](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Openreach_Fibre_Broadband_Street_Cabinet%2C_Rural_Appearance.jpg)

## What Ofcom decides next

Ofcom's position is that Openreach earned more commercial freedom through its own wholesale market review concluded earlier this year, which set the current rules for how the dominant network operator can compete on price. A spokesman said the regulator is now assessing whether the specific discounts raise competition concerns serious enough to warrant intervention, with a consultation due for publication later this month.

The UK broadband market has roughly 100 alternative network builders jostling for a shrinking pool of undecided customers, and consolidation among them has accelerated as smaller altnets run short of capital. Openreach retains by far the largest network footprint and, crucially, the deepest relationships with the resellers who decide where new customers actually get connected. Whether Ofcom treats Openreach's rebates as legitimate competitive response or anti-competitive foreclosure will shape how much room is left for challengers like Virgin Media O2 to build scale — and that answer, alongside the CMA's Netomnia ruling in December, will do more to determine the shape of Britain's fibre market than any discount headline on its own.

airbus-getafe-strike.headline: Airbus deliveries slip as Getafe strike drags on
airbus-getafe-strike.body_md:
Airbus's problem this month is not demand. It is getting airplanes out the door. At the company's Getafe engineering and manufacturing site outside Madrid, roughly 3,000 of the plant's 9,000 workers have been on strike since July 1, and the walkout has begun to snarl the aircraft inspections and engineering checks that sit between a finished airframe and a delivered one — the paperwork-and-signoff stage that airlines and lessors will not skip, strike or no strike.

The action was called by SIPA, the second-largest union at Airbus's Spanish operations, and has since drawn in UGT, the country's national trade union confederation. Getafe is Airbus's third-largest site worldwide and handles horizontal stabilisers and rear-fuselage sections for the A320, A330 and A350 families, along with military and space engineering work — not glamorous, but structurally load-bearing in the literal and financial sense. Participation across Airbus's roughly 14,000 employees in Spain has reportedly reached 80% on strike days, according to Spanish outlet Getafe Central, spreading beyond Getafe to Airbus Defence and Space and Airbus Helicopters España sites in the same municipality.

![Airbus's engineering and manufacturing plant in Getafe, near Madrid](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/80/AIRBUS.Getafe.SPAIN.2013.06.08.jpg)

## What the strikers want

The grievances are the familiar shape of a labor dispute at a company posting record profits — Airbus reported €5.22 billion in net income for 2025 — while asking staff to absorb tighter terms. Airbus set 2026 and 2027 pay increases unilaterally at 3% and 2% after talks stalled, figures workers say lag inflation. From September, office staff will be required in four days a week rather than three, cutting a day of remote work. The company has also moved to end the 100% salary top-up during short-term sick leave, introduced a stricter absenteeism-tracking method known as the Bradford Index, and fixed three weeks of August vacation that were previously negotiated with more flexibility. None of these are the kind of number that shows up in a 10-K. All of them are the kind of number that shows up in a picket line.

SIPA has called the action through July 31. More consequential for anyone modeling the rest of the year: Comisiones Obreras, or CCOO, the largest union at Airbus's Spanish plants, sat out this round but has said it will call an indefinite strike from September 7 if talks fail, warning that deliveries would be "seriously affected" across all Spanish plants in the last four months of 2026. That is the scenario worth tracking, since a month-long July strike and an open-ended one starting in the autumn are different orders of risk entirely.

## A guidance number already under strain

The timing lands badly. Airbus has told investors to expect around 870 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2026, a target that was already sitting on shaky ground before a single Getafe worker walked out. The company delivered at a run rate of roughly 71 aircraft a month in the first half of the second quarter, according to analysis cited by AskTraders, but that pace had slipped to about 42 a month by mid-May — well short of what's needed. Hitting 870 for the year now requires roughly 97 deliveries a month for the remainder of 2026, a pace mwb Research analyst Jens-Peter Rieck called "the strongest second half in company history."

![A Lufthansa Airbus A320neo, the aircraft family whose components are built at Getafe](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Lufthansa_Airbus_A320neo.jpg)

Rieck has gone further, describing Airbus as caught in a "credibility squeeze": the company is maintaining its 870-unit guidance in public while simultaneously freezing 10% of non-industrial spending internally — a combination he called difficult to reconcile, and evidence that Airbus's existing LEAD cost-reduction program, launched in 2024, has "proven insufficient." His house view is that a formal cut toward roughly 840 deliveries is "a matter of when, not if." That call predates the Getafe strike; the walkout adds a fresh, difficult-to-quantify drag on top of an already-strained production system, one already complicated separately by Pratt & Whitney's reluctance to commit firmly to engine delivery numbers for the year, per comments from chief executive Guillaume Faury in February.

## Why a stabiliser plant matters to a delivery count

The mechanics matter here. Getafe does not build complete aircraft — final assembly happens in Toulouse, Hamburg, Mobile and Tianjin — so the strike will not directly halt an assembly line the way a walkout at those sites would. But horizontal stabilisers and fuselage sections built at Getafe feed those lines, and the engineering sign-offs performed there are gating steps for aircraft further along in the process. Airbus has reportedly already begun shifting some engineering work to other subsidiaries to keep programs moving, according to Spanish outlet El Independiente — a workaround that buys time but does not replace lost capacity for free. Delivery slippage of this kind rarely shows up as a single dramatic cancellation; it shows up as aircraft sitting a few weeks longer in pre-delivery configuration, revenue recognition pushed a quarter later than modeled, and a delivery count that quietly misses guidance by enough to move a rating.

For a company whose backlog stretches past nine years of production at current rates — 9,247 aircraft as of the end of May, split heavily toward the A320neo family — the strike is not an existential threat to the order book. It is a test of execution at exactly the moment execution was already the thing analysts were worried about.

## What comes next

The SIPA-led strike runs through the end of July, after which the more consequential date is September 7: the deadline CCOO has set before calling an indefinite strike across all Spanish plants. Airbus's next scheduled update on production and delivery pace will show whether the run rate has recovered toward the roughly 97-a-month pace needed to hit 870 for the year, or whether Rieck's predicted guidance cut toward 840 arrives first. Either way, the Getafe dispute has turned a spreadsheet debate about delivery cadence into a labor negotiation with a hard deadline attached.

solar-developer-bankruptcy.headline: Renewable energy developer collapses into bankruptcy months after signing new deals
solar-developer-bankruptcy.body_md:
In February, GoldenPeaks Capital was closing one of the largest corporate solar deals in Hungary's history — a ten-year agreement to supply Hankook Tire's Rácalmás plant with 430 gigawatt-hours of power from 30 megawatts of new photovoltaic capacity, enough to cover a fifth of the tire maker's electricity use there. It followed a run of similar contracts with Nestlé, Cargill, Mars, Mondelez and Auchan, the kind of blue-chip roster that lets a renewable developer claim it has arrived. GoldenPeaks, by then one of the largest solar owner-operators in Poland and Hungary with a construction pipeline exceeding a gigawatt, looked like a company built for the corporate clean-power boom.

Five months later it was in Chapter 11.

![Photovoltaic panels at a solar farm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e2/Photovoltaic_Panels_at_the_Travers_Solar_Farm.jpg)

## A liquidity crisis measured in weeks, not years

GoldenPeaks Poland Holding, the Malta-domiciled parent of the group's Polish and Hungarian solar assets, filed for bankruptcy protection on May 29 in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas, along with 39 affiliated entities. The filing listed roughly $952 million in funded debt against a cash position of less than €1.1 million — a company that had, at its peak, run the largest utility-scale solar portfolio in Poland and employed more than 250 people, reduced to unable to meet payroll.

Edward Manning of Alvarez & Marsal, the restructuring adviser brought in to manage the collapse, told the court the deterioration was "precipitous": liquidity "evaporated" within weeks, a payroll cycle was missed, staff walked out, and events of default cascaded across more than twenty separate financing facilities almost simultaneously. Court filings describe a company with no direct employees of its own by the time of filing, running entirely on three outside contractors — Alvarez & Marsal for restructuring, Ergy for asset management, and PwC for back-office functions — a structure that left GoldenPeaks with strikingly little internal capacity to manage a crisis once one began.

The immediate trigger was the January collapse of Spectris Energy, the contractor that handled essentially all of GoldenPeaks' operations, maintenance, engineering and construction work. Spectris entered its own remedial insolvency proceedings after component costs and currency swings made its contracts unworkable, and Polish tax authorities froze its bank accounts — disrupting both the solar farms already running and the ones still being built. "GoldenPeaks had nobody left to run its solar farms," as one account of the case put it. Layer on top of that: curtailment orders from Poland's grid operator limiting how much power the company's plants could actually sell, construction and financing costs that ran ahead of projections through 2025 and 2026, a paused equity raise in the first quarter of this year for lack of investor interest, and — according to filings — internal accounting so disordered that standalone financial statements hadn't been produced and ledgers were unclosed since December.

## The Brookfield fight

What has made the case unusually contentious is the role of Brookfield Asset Management, GoldenPeaks' controlling shareholder since a roughly €8.5 million investment years earlier that grew into a roughly $294 million junior secured lending position. Brookfield holds two of five board seats, extended a $12 million emergency bridge loan in early May as the crisis peaked, and has now proposed a $162.8 million debtor-in-possession loan to fund the four-month restructuring — while simultaneously positioning itself as the stalking-horse lead bidder for GoldenPeaks' assets in the court-supervised auction that loan is meant to finance.

![Aerial view of the Hankook Tire plant in Rácalmás, Hungary](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Hankook_Tire%2C_R%C3%A1calm%C3%A1s.jpg)

That dual role drew a sharp objection from Berenberg, the German merchant bank whose Alternative Assets Fund II sits as a mezzanine lender structurally senior to some of Brookfield's positions. Berenberg's lawyers accused Brookfield of trying to "jump ahead of structurally senior creditors" and of "secretly establishing US jurisdiction" over the case by routing a European asset group through a Texas courtroom, and flagged the DIP loan's terms — cross-collateralization without carve-outs, no adequate protection for existing lenders — as tilting the eventual sale in Brookfield's favor before other bidders got a look. US Bankruptcy Judge Alfredo Perez rejected the challenge on July 6, approving Brookfield as both DIP lender and lead bidder and clearing the way for a $114.8 million debt-for-assets bid to anchor the auction. Berenberg has reserved its right to contest jurisdiction and venue as the case proceeds.

## What it says about corporate clean-power deals

The uncomfortable detail in the GoldenPeaks case is not that a leveraged developer ran into trouble — that happens. It's the compression of the timeline. A company signing new long-term supply contracts with a Fortune Global 500 tire manufacturer in February was insolvent by May. Corporate power purchase agreements have become the preferred vehicle for companies like Nestlé, Cargill, Mars and Hankook to hit their own climate targets without owning generation assets themselves: the buyer locks in a price, the developer takes on the construction and operating risk, and everyone gets a line for the sustainability report. GoldenPeaks' PPA counterparties are not directly on the hook for its debt, and the underlying solar assets — panels already spinning revenue under contract — are exactly what Brookfield is bidding to keep running. But the speed of the collapse is a reminder that a signed PPA is a claim on a counterparty's future solvency, not just its megawatts, and that the credit quality behind these deals doesn't always get the scrutiny that the headline contract announcement does.

For Brookfield, the case is a small entry in a much larger book: the firm has raised over $40 billion for decarbonization investing since 2021 and already holds a stake in Poland's Polenergia. For GoldenPeaks' other lenders and its corporate offtakers, the next milestone is more immediate. The court-supervised auction Brookfield is now positioned to win is expected to run through the four-month DIP financing window, meaning a sale — or a further fight over who controls the assets — should land by late autumn.

easyjet-pe-bidding-war.headline: EasyJet takeover battle pulls private equity out of its comfort zone
easyjet-pe-bidding-war.body_md:
EasyJet has spent two decades being the airline private equity firms politely avoided. Thin margins, brutal fuel exposure, a habit of losing money whenever the world does something unexpected — none of it fit the buyout playbook. Over the past twenty years, PE firms globally have announced only about $8 billion in airline deals, roughly 2% of all transport and logistics spending, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data. That history is why the fight now unfolding over EasyJet is being read on trading floors less as an airline story than as a private equity story.

![A G-EZDP Airbus A319 in EasyJet livery takes off from Amsterdam Schiphol](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/17/G-EZDP_-_Airbus_A319-111_-_EasyJet_takeoff_from_Schiphol_pic1.JPG)

EasyJet said on Friday it had agreed in principle to a cash offer from Apollo Global Management worth £5.7 billion, or £7.15 a share — trumping a £6.90-a-share bid from fellow U.S. fund Castlelake that the airline's board had accepted just days earlier, on July 7. Apollo's offer is an 81% premium to the £3.94 EasyJet shares fetched on May 28, the last trading day before Castlelake's interest became public. The stock jumped 13% on the news. Apollo now has until August 7 under U.K. takeover rules to make a firm offer or walk away.

## Why airlines, why now

The honest answer has less to do with EasyJet than with the roughly $2.5 trillion in private equity dry powder sitting uninvested worldwide, about $1 trillion of it in the U.S. Buyout funds typically have a five-year window to deploy committed capital, and the clock is running out on money raised in the fundraising boom of the early 2020s: 24% of global buyout dry powder has now sat unspent for four years or more, up from 20% in 2022, according to industry data. Limited partners want distributions, not idle commitments, and the inventory of conventional buyout targets — mid-market industrials, software roll-ups, healthcare services — has been picked over.

"Nearly every decade seems to bring an unexpected shock of some kind," Paolo Battaglia of Lazard said of the airline sector. "That makes underwriting airline risk difficult for buyout firms." That risk hasn't gone away — EasyJet's pre-tax loss widened to £552 million in the first half of 2026, with the airline citing higher fuel costs and weaker forward bookings tied to the Middle East conflict. What has changed is the tolerance for it, because the alternative is capital that earns nothing at all.

Apollo brings a track record here that Castlelake, an aviation-leasing specialist better known for financing aircraft than running them, does not: it has restructured distressed carriers before, steering Aeromexico back to profitability by 2023 and doing similar work at Sun Country, largely by stripping out premium features and running a leaner cost base. That playbook — treat an airline like any other overleveraged industrial asset, cut hard, sell ancillary revenue aggressively — is presumably the pitch Apollo is making to EasyJet's board about why this time is different.

## The EU complication

Both bidders face the same regulatory obstacle: EU law requires airlines flying within the bloc to be majority-owned and effectively controlled by EU member states or qualifying European nationals, a rule that predates Brexit but now applies to EasyJet's continental operations in a way that bites harder for two American funds. Castlelake had proposed satisfying it by installing two Irish aviation executives — Peter Bellew, a former EasyJet chief operating officer, and Mark Breen, chief executive of Dublin-based Oneiros Aerospace — as controlling shareholders through an EU-based vehicle. Apollo has said only that it will take "all necessary steps" to secure merger clearance and satisfy the EU's Foreign Subsidies Regulation, without yet detailing how it clears the ownership bar.

Bloomberg Intelligence's Conroy Gaynor noted that EasyJet "has generally traded at a significant discount since travel fully resumed after the pandemic" — the kind of valuation gap that makes a takeover premium easier to justify on paper, whatever the underlying business is doing. Jefferies' Sheila Kahyaoglu offered the more optimistic frame: European budget carriers are, on their own operating merits, a segment that "tend[s] to do really well."

## What it signals

A bidding war for a loss-making, low-margin airline is not, by itself, evidence that airlines have become safer investments. It is better read as evidence that the buyout industry's usual hunting grounds are thinning out, and that firms sitting on aging, unspent capital are being pushed toward assets they would once have passed on. If Apollo can prove out its restructuring thesis on EasyJet the way it did at Aeromexico, the deal recasts the sector as investable. If not, it becomes the latest reminder — after SAS, after Alitalia, after a long list of carriers that burned outside capital — of why private equity avoided airlines in the first place.

The near-term marker is August 7, Apollo's deadline to convert its indicative offer into a firm one under U.K. takeover rules. Watch also for whether Castlelake returns with a sixth revised bid, and for the first concrete detail from Apollo on how it intends to satisfy the EU's ownership-and-control test — the one obstacle that neither fund's balance sheet can simply outbid.

burnham-uk-pm.headline: Andy Burnham set to become UK prime minister as policy agenda stays unclear
burnham-uk-pm.body_md:
Sometime around midday on July 20, Andy Burnham will travel to Buckingham Palace, be received by King Charles III, and return to Downing Street as the United Kingdom's prime minister. Barring a rival candidacy that has not materialised and looks unlikely to, the mechanics of the handover are no longer in doubt. What remains genuinely unclear — to Labour MPs, to the civil service, and to the investors who price UK debt every morning — is what he intends to do once he gets there.

That gap between political certainty and policy uncertainty is the story. Keir Starmer's departure ends a fractious three years in charge of a party that never fully reconciled itself to his leadership; Burnham's arrival begins a premiership whose economic instincts are, by most accounts, still being worked out inside a small circle of advisers rather than road-tested in public.

![Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham together during a Manchester school visit in April 2026, months before the leadership handover](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0a/Keir_Starmer_and_Andy_Burnham_%2855204794065%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A resignation that had been building for months

Starmer announced on June 22 that he would step down, capping a slide in authority that accelerated after Labour's poor showing in May's local elections. The proximate trigger came days earlier: Burnham, until then serving as mayor of Greater Manchester and shut out of the leadership race by a party rule requiring candidates to sit in the Commons, won the Makerfield by-election on June 18 by a wider margin than expected. The seat had been vacated specifically to clear his path back to Westminster — a manoeuvre that only makes sense if the people arranging it already believed Starmer's position was terminal.

It was the UK's now-familiar pattern of leadership churn, this time playing out inside a governing party rather than between elections. Nominations for the Labour leadership opened July 9 and close July 16; within the first day, 322 MPs — well over 80% of the parliamentary party — had publicly nominated Burnham, with potential rivals including Wes Streeting, Darren Jones and Al Carns all ruling themselves out. That scale of support made it structurally impossible for anyone else to reach the 81 nominations needed to appear on a ballot. A special conference on July 17 is expected to confirm him as Labour leader without a contest, ahead of the formal transfer of power on July 20.

## What Burnham has and hasn't said

The uncontested nature of the coronation has had a curious side effect: with no rival to draw out his positions in debate, Burnham has faced less pressure than a contested leadership race would normally generate to specify what he'd actually do in office. His public remarks lean toward devolving greater fiscal authority to regional governments — a natural extension of his mayoral record — and restructuring aspects of national governance, but the detail behind both ideas remains sparse even to some of his own allies.

On tax, he has been notably difficult to pin down. He has floated openness to a land value tax, arguing UK property is undertaxed relative to income, and has signalled he might revisit capital gains tax treatment. On a wealth tax proper, he has avoided a firm no while making clear it "wouldn't be a priority." A proposal to restructure the Treasury was reportedly considered and then dropped. Taken together, these are the fragments of a philosophy — shift the tax burden from income toward assets and property — rather than a costed programme.

![The Bank of England on Threadneedle Street, whose fiscal-rules framework Burnham has pledged to keep](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/Bank_of_England_Threadneedle_St._%2812565194585%29.jpg)

## Markets are pricing the ambiguity, not the ideology

Bond and currency markets have responded less to what Burnham believes than to how firmly he's committed to existing constraints. When he used a major speech to tie himself explicitly to "the discipline of our current fiscal rules" — the framework Rachel Reeves built after the 2022 Truss crisis to keep gilt investors calm — the reaction was mild relief: 30-year gilt yields eased two basis points and sterling firmed to $1.3240. But that calm didn't hold. In the week after his emphatic Makerfield win, gilts sold off again, with the 10-year yield rising and sterling softening, as traders concluded that a prime minister with a personal mandate this large might feel less bound by rules he inherited than one who negotiated them.

John Stopford of asset manager Ninety One captured the market's working assumption: any incoming government, whatever its rhetoric, "will still face fiscal constraints." The nuance investors are watching for is subtler than rule-compliance — gilt investors have made clear that meeting the fiscal rules on paper is necessary but not sufficient. What actually moves gilt yields on Budget day is the volume of debt the Debt Management Office plans to issue, not the political justification attached to it. A Burnham government that keeps the rules intact but leans on creative accounting to expand headroom would face the same scrutiny as one that changed the rules outright.

## What's next

The near-term calendar is now fixed: the special conference on July 17, the handover on July 20, and a cabinet reshuffle expected to follow within days — the choice of chancellor will be read by markets as the clearest early signal of intent, more than anything Burnham says in a leadership speech. Beyond that, the first fiscal event of his premiership, whenever the Treasury schedules it, will be the moment the ambiguity has to resolve into numbers: a spending envelope, an issuance remit, and an answer on whether the fiscal rules he has pledged to keep are being kept in substance or merely in name.

once-upon-a-farm-fair-value-cut.headline: Once Upon A Farm's fair value cut 10% after analyst reset
once-upon-a-farm-fair-value-cut.body_md:
Analysts tracking Once Upon A Farm PBC have trimmed the average 12-month fair value estimate for the stock to $24.38, down from $27.13 — a roughly 10% reset compiled by Simply Wall St. from the models of firms including TD Cowen and Barclays. The company, the organic baby-food maker co-founded by Jennifer Garner and now-CEO John Foraker, went public on the New York Stock Exchange on February 6 this year, pricing its IPO at $18 a share and closing its debut day up 17%.

The reset traces to a specific event rather than a vague vibe shift. Once Upon A Farm's first earnings report as a public company, on May 7, showed solid 2025 numbers but a 2026 sales outlook of $302 million to $310 million — growth of 25% to 29%, a sharp deceleration from the 53% expansion the company posted the year before. Adjusted EBITDA guidance of just $2 million to $4 million left little room to argue the business is turning a corner on profitability. Shares fell roughly 7% on the print and have since traded as low as $14, well off the $27 high they touched earlier in the year.

TD Cowen and Barclays both cut targets in the reset that produced the new $24.38 consensus — TD Cowen's move accounting for roughly $8 of the reduction, Barclays for about $5 — while continuing coverage rather than dropping the stock. Evercore ISI and Deutsche Bank have also lowered targets since the print, to $23 and $17 respectively, with ratings that read more "wait and see" than "sell." Simply Wall St.'s own discounted-cash-flow inputs shifted alongside the target cuts: the model's forward price-to-earnings multiple came down to 41.7 times from 52.4 times, even as projected revenue growth and margins ticked up slightly. In plain terms, the earnings power hasn't obviously worsened — analysts have simply decided they should pay less for it.

## Company problem, or sector problem?

That distinction matters for reading across to the rest of consumer staples. Once Upon A Farm's cut lands alongside a broader bout of analyst caution in packaged food: Stephens downgraded Campbell Soup to Equal Weight from Overweight in June and cut its target to $21 from $28, citing margin pressure from heavier promotional spending, and Simply Good Foods has drawn similar scrutiny over declining Atkins sales. But the through-line at those companies is margin compression in mature, competitive categories — not the growth-deceleration story driving Once Upon A Farm's reset. A five-month-old IPO burning through its growth premium is a different animal from a decades-old soup brand losing pricing power. The honest read is that this is a company-specific repricing of a newly public growth story that arrived amid, rather than because of, a jittery moment for food stocks generally.

The next real test comes September 2, when Once Upon A Farm reports second-quarter results. Whether net sales growth tracks toward the low or high end of that 25-to-29% guidance range — and whether adjusted EBITDA clears even the low end of its $2 million to $4 million range — will do more to settle the valuation question than any further round of target trims.

astrazeneca-2030-targets-revised.headline: AstraZeneca scales back some 2030 sustainability targets
astrazeneca-2030-targets-revised.body_md:
AstraZeneca has trimmed two of its headline 2030 sustainability commitments, telling investors and analysts this week that the changes reflect the pharmaceutical giant's growth trajectory and lessons learned from five years of running the programmes — not a retreat from the goals themselves.

The company's near-term Scope 3 emissions target — covering indirect emissions across its supply chain, from raw materials to how patients use its products — has been revised down to a 35% cut versus 2019 levels, from a prior goal of 50%. Separately, its AZ Forest tree-planting initiative, launched in 2020, now targets 100 million trees by 2030, half the original 200 million goal.

![AstraZeneca's headquarters and R&D centre at Cambridge Biomedical Campus, UK](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/AstraZeneca_HQ_in_Cambridge_UK.jpg)

> "Operating sustainably is good for business and core to operating a responsible, efficient, and resilient business for the long term."

That was Pam Cheng, AstraZeneca's chief sustainability officer, in the company's update, which also pointed to a company case for keeping the emissions math intact even as the percentage target shrinks: because the business has grown substantially since 2019 — AstraZeneca is chasing $80 billion in revenue and 20 new medicines by 2030 — the absolute tonnage of emissions the company expects to cut under the new 35% target is roughly the same as it would have removed hitting 50% against the smaller, 2019-era revenue base. In other words, a bigger company doing proportionally less still nets out to a similar amount of carbon.

## Growth versus green math

The tree target tells a more straightforward story of a company recalibrating an ambition that outran its execution capacity. AstraZeneca has planted just over 66 million trees across 80 species since 2020 — roughly a third of the way to the original 200 million goal with less than a third of the timeline remaining. Management framed the reduction as a shift toward "high-quality projects rather than volume," language that reads as an admission that scaling tree planting to that size, credibly and verifiably, proved harder than initially modelled.

Elsewhere, the company pointed to progress it says justifies confidence in the revised targets: an 88% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions — the ones from its own operations and energy use — as of December 2025, an $500 million investment to replace propellants in its inhalers with a near-zero-warming alternative (inhalers alone account for about a quarter of the company's Scope 3 footprint), and 81% of its global vehicle fleet now electric.

## AI as both lever and liability

Artificial intelligence featured heavily in the update, cast simultaneously as a tool for hitting sustainability goals and a driver of the business growth that necessitated recalibrating them. AstraZeneca said it is using AI to model drug candidates digitally, targeting roughly a 35% productivity improvement and 50% faster development lead times by 2030 — fewer wasted lab cycles and physical trial runs, in theory, translate into a lighter environmental footprint per drug brought to market. The company also cited MILTON, an AI system trained on UK Biobank data that it says can predict risk across more than 1,000 conditions, in some cases 10 to 15 years before clinical diagnosis, which it frames as reducing downstream healthcare resource use through earlier intervention.

At the same time, AstraZeneca acknowledged that the computing power behind its AI push carries its own emissions cost, and said it is shifting data-centre infrastructure toward energy-efficient, renewable-powered capacity, alongside a formal governance process requiring approval for public AI tools and ongoing validation of higher-risk systems.

## What it signals

For ESG-oriented investors, the revision is a useful data point in a broader pattern: large-cap companies are quietly loosening self-imposed climate targets as AI infrastructure spending competes for capital and management attention. AstraZeneca is not abandoning its 2030 framework, and its Scope 1 and 2 progress is real and independently verifiable. But a target that shrinks from 50% to 35% — even with an absolute-tonnage justification attached — will read to some fund screens as a downgrade, regardless of the accounting rationale offered.

The update lands within days of a separate, far larger shock to AstraZeneca's market value after a drug trial setback wiped tens of billions off its share price — a reminder that sustainability targets, however carefully calibrated, sit well down the list of what is currently moving the stock. The next real test comes when AstraZeneca reports full-year 2026 progress against the revised targets, and whether the "lessons learned" framing holds up to scrutiny from ESG raters recalculating their models in the meantime.

ukraine-long-range-command.headline: Ukraine creates long-range strike command to hit Russian energy infrastructure
ukraine-long-range-command.body_md:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree this week creating a dedicated "long-range impact" command inside Ukraine's armed forces — a bureaucratic-sounding move with a blunt purpose. It consolidates the drone units, planning staff and targeting intelligence behind more than a year of deep strikes into a single chain of command, one built to keep hitting the refineries, pipelines and depots that fund Russia's war.

"Today, I signed a decree establishing a special command within the Armed Forces," Zelenskyy said in his evening address, "a command aimed at a long-range and, in effect, global impact on Russia in response to this war." Ukrainian officials have described the new structure's mandate in blunter terms still: to put 100% of available resources behind reducing Russia's capacity to sustain the fighting.

![Volodymyr Zelensky, official portrait](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/69/Volodymyr_Zelensky_Official_portrait_%28cropped_2048x2048_px%29.jpg)

## A war economy already under strain

What makes the announcement more than symbolic is the campaign it now formalizes. Ukrainian long-range drones — chiefly the Fire Point-built FP-1, a one-way attack aircraft with a stated range of 1,600 kilometers and a warhead of up to 120 kilograms — have hit more than a dozen major Russian refineries and fuel terminals since the start of the year, some more than 2,500 kilometers from the border. On July 6, drones reportedly struck the Gazprom Neft refinery at Omsk, Russia's largest, disabling equipment responsible for as much as 40% of the plant's output. Nizhnekamsk and Saratov were hit within the following 48 hours.

The cumulative effect shows up in Russian fuel markets rather than any single dramatic strike. Independent estimates suggest the attacks have knocked out somewhere between a fifth and two-fifths of Russian refining capacity, leaving domestic gasoline output running roughly 20% below demand. Moscow has already banned exports of petrol and jet fuel and is weighing the same for diesel — a step it took in part because of a lingering fuel shortage in occupied Crimea, where rationing at filling stations has become routine. The International Energy Agency has trimmed its forecast for Russian oil output by 85,000 barrels a day this year and 150,000 next.

![Gazprom Neft's high-tech refining complex in Omsk, seen from above](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/84/%D0%92%D1%8B%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%B5%D1%85%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%B8%D1%87%D0%BD%D1%8B%D0%B9_%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BC%D0%BF%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BA%D1%81_%D0%B3%D0%BB%D1%83%D0%B1%D0%BE%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B9_%D0%BF%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B1%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%BA%D0%B8_%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%84%D1%82%D0%B8_%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%9D%D0%9F%D0%97_%C2%AB%D0%93%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%84%D1%82%D0%B8%C2%BB_%D0%B2_%D0%9E%D0%BC%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B5.jpg)

## The sea campaign nobody predicted

The newer front is maritime. Robert Brovdi — known by the callsign "Madyar," and commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces — has reported a rapid escalation of strikes on the so-called shadow fleet of aging tankers Russia uses to move sanctioned oil. In a single 72-hour stretch this month, Ukrainian forces claimed to have hit 21 vessels in the Sea of Azov, most of them tankers, alongside tugboats and cargo ships supporting Crimea's supply lines. Russia has responded by suspending navigation through the Don–Azov canal and telling shipping firms it would stop processing passage requests through the Kerch Strait — a disruption that has also snarled grain exports from southern Russia, a secondary effect Kyiv has not been shy about advertising.

Taken together, the refinery strikes and the tanker campaign are two expressions of the same theory: that Ukraine, unable to match Russia's manpower or match it missile-for-missile, can still bleed the revenue and logistics that keep the war funded. Officials in Kyiv have taken to calling it a form of "long-range sanctions," a phrase meant to underline that the target is Russia's war chest rather than its front lines.

## What the new command changes, and what it doesn't

It is worth being precise about what this week's decree actually does. It does not introduce a new weapon or a new capability — the FP-1 and its naval-drone counterparts already existed, and Brovdi's forces were already running the tanker strikes. What changes is organizational: authority over long-range operations moves under one roof, with a mandate that outranks competing claims on drones, intelligence and production capacity. Military analysts caution that it remains unclear whether even a more efficient campaign can alter the war's trajectory on its own — Russia continues to launch missile and drone barrages of its own, and Ukraine's air defenses remain stretched.

For markets, the relevant question is less about a single battlefield decision and more about durability. A one-off refinery fire is noise; sustained double-digit reductions in Russian refining capacity, an export ban that spreads from diesel to crude products, and a shadow fleet that operators increasingly regard as uninsurable are the kind of frictions that show up in global diesel and gasoil spreads even without moving Brent much on their own. The IEA's downward revisions to Russian output are an early signal of that shift, small in absolute terms but pointed in direction.

The next things to watch are concrete rather than rhetorical: whether Moscow extends its export ban to diesel, whether the Kerch Strait disruption starts showing up in Black Sea grain-shipment data, and whether the new command's first weeks bring a change in strike tempo or simply a change in the org chart signing off on it.

c3ai-siebel-return-revenue-slide.headline: C3.ai's revenue slide collides with Tom Siebel's return and a bigger Shell deal
c3ai-siebel-return-revenue-slide.body_md:
Tom Siebel has run C3.ai twice now, and both times he came back to a company whose numbers didn't match its narrative. The first time, in the late 1990s echo of enterprise software, the story was growth. This time, the enterprise AI vendor he founded in 2009 just posted a 35% revenue decline for the fiscal year, a widening loss, and a leadership saga that ended with the 73-year-old founder reclaiming the chief executive's chair he'd handed off nine months earlier. Three weeks after that, Shell — one of C3.ai's oldest and largest customers — signed up for more.

The two facts sit awkwardly together. A company whose revenue is falling by more than a third is not, on its face, a company energy majors should be expanding their bets on. Yet that is exactly what happened, and the contradiction is the story: nobody, including the analysts paid to model this stuff, seems to agree on whether C3.ai's enterprise AI software actually works well enough to justify what customers and investors are being asked to pay for it.

## A revolving door in the corner office

Siebel stepped back from the CEO role in mid-2025 after disclosing an autoimmune condition that had damaged his eyesight. Stephen Ehikian, a Salesforce veteran and former acting administrator of the U.S. General Services Administration, took over as CEO on September 1, 2025, while Siebel stayed on as executive chairman. That arrangement lasted eight months. On May 8, 2026, C3.ai announced Siebel was resuming the CEO title, with Ehikian shifting to president.

"While my vision remains impaired, it is improving," Siebel said in the announcement. "The health issues I encountered during 2025 are largely resolved." He called himself "energized to be back in the CEO role."

![Thomas Siebel, founder and CEO of C3.ai, pictured in 2013](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Tom_Siebel_2013.png)

The reinstatement came bundled with a signal investors don't often get: Siebel personally bought 6.17 million newly issued shares directly from the company at $11.16 apiece, putting roughly $69 million in fresh cash on C3.ai's balance sheet and lifting total cash and marketable securities to about $673 million. It's a notable reversal — earlier in 2026, while serving as executive chairman rather than CEO, Siebel had sold several million dollars of stock, including a $7.6 million sale in January and a $4.4 million sale in March. Insiders selling into weakness and then buying back in at a founder's return is not unheard of, but it does little to settle the question of what Siebel actually believes about the stock's near-term prospects versus its long-term one.

## The numbers Siebel came back to

Whatever confidence the share purchase was meant to convey, the fiscal year he inherited was rough by any measure. C3.ai's total revenue for the fiscal year ended April 30, 2026 came to $250.3 million, down 35% from the prior year. The fourth quarter alone told a starker story: $51.6 million in revenue, down from $108.7 million in the same quarter a year earlier — a decline of more than half. GAAP loss from operations for the full year widened to $498.5 million; on a non-GAAP basis, the operating loss was $217.8 million.

C3.ai has responded with a restructuring plan the company says will generate about $135 million in annualized non-GAAP cost savings and cut cash burn by a similar amount. That's a meaningful retrenchment for a company whose pitch to Wall Street has for years rested on enterprise AI as a growth category, not a cost-cutting one. Investors, for their part, were unmoved by the leadership change: C3.ai shares fell roughly 7% on the news of Siebel's return, part of a stock that was already down around a fifth for the year.

## What Shell sees that Wall Street doesn't

Against that backdrop, Shell's decision to deepen its relationship with C3.ai reads almost like a counter-argument. The two companies have worked together since 2018, when Shell adopted C3 AI's predictive-maintenance software to monitor more than 13,000 pieces of equipment across upstream, midstream and downstream operations on six continents — refineries, offshore platforms, pipelines. Shell renewed the partnership for five years in 2021. On June 4, 2026, the companies announced a new multi-year expansion: Shell will layer AI agent-based root-cause analysis and remediation, built on C3.ai's Agentic AI Platform and running on Microsoft Azure, on top of the existing reliability monitoring.

![Shell's Pernis refinery in the Netherlands, one of the sites within the scope of Shell's predictive-maintenance program](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Shell_Pernis_refinery_2019.jpg)

Shell is not a customer prone to sentimentality about vendor relationships; oil majors run tight procurement processes and can walk away from underperforming software with little friction. That it chose to expand — after seven years of production use across a genuinely large industrial footprint — is real evidence that C3.ai's product works for at least one of the hardest use cases in enterprise software: physical asset reliability at global scale. It just isn't evidence that the product is selling well enough, broadly enough, to keep the company's revenue line moving in the right direction.

## The valuation question nobody has answered

Wall Street's read on all this is, fittingly, split down the middle. The consensus analyst rating on C3.ai is a Hold, with price targets scattered from roughly $11 to $16 a share. A price-to-sales comparison against peers suggests the stock is still priced for a growth rate it isn't delivering, and one widely cited discounted-cash-flow estimate puts it as much as 35% overvalued. Gross margins remain below 40%, well short of what a mature enterprise software business typically carries.

That gap — between a marquee customer doubling down and a market that can't decide what the stock is worth — is the real takeaway. Enterprise AI vendors have spent three years selling Fortune 500 boards on the idea that predictive models and AI agents pay for themselves in avoided downtime and labor savings. Shell's expanded contract is a data point that the technology can deliver on that promise in at least one demanding setting. C3.ai's own income statement is a data point that turning technical wins into a durable, profitable business is a separate and much harder problem. The next test comes with C3.ai's first-quarter fiscal 2027 results, expected in early September, when investors will find out whether the restructuring and the founder's return have done anything to slow the revenue slide — or whether Shell's vote of confidence remains an outlier rather than a signal.

floor.headline: Two for three, but conviction proved no guarantee
floor.body_md: The day broke predictably for WMT and HSY, less so for AIV. WMT's mild-oversold bounce unfolded as planned—RSI resolved toward the 20-day SMA over a 5-day hold already underway at entry, no news interference, no surprises. HSY trailed along with a smaller gain. But AIV, carrying the highest conviction score (0.7) on the deepest oversold read in the basket (RSI 20.4), never budged from 2.80. The setup was sound. The market's answer was indifference. A modest +0.63% average return overall, but the spread between conviction and outcome raises a question for tomorrow: if single-session holds are too narrow for oversold reversions to play out, does the bot need longer windows or a new signal?

floor.headline: Thesis Confirmed, Trades Didn't
floor.body_md: The macro thesis was textbook — financials sector strength confirmed (XLF +1.39% through the week), ABN.AS showing relative resilience with a clean technical breakout. Then the actual trades happened. HOOD bore the brunt of the day's damage, down 3% to stop after reversing almost immediately on entry. The Barclays PT raise and sector strength proved immaterial. ABN.AS and MUV2.DE drifted sideways in smaller losses, confirming the pattern: sector strength on tape doesn't guarantee individual follow-through. The thesis was sound; the execution wasn't. Tomorrow needs tighter entries or higher conviction before committing to the trade.
